artist.heading: I build spatial interfaces, web systems, and visual stories
body: I'm currently working as a research assistant at HKUST VISLab, exploring XR and HCI for immersive learning, and as a freelance creative technologist, building interactive prototypes and media systems for clients.
The through-line is hands-on craft: Unity scenes, interface logic, motion, narrative structure, and the small technical decisions that make an experience feel understandable.

projects.title: Midnight at the Pagoda
projects.role: VR R&D project / HCI Research Thesis

coverMedia.alt: Rendered pagoda exhibition scene with warm interior lighting and red architectural elements

projects.tagline: A vertical museum journey built as both a VR app and a study environment for embodied memory.

projectFacts.label: Project Type
projectFacts.value: Research thesis evolved from a hackathon prototype

projectFacts.label: Results
value: The Best Use of Tech Award, Digital Heritage 2024

projects.detailHeading: A VR heritage app and research thesis studying how artifact interaction changes what visitors remember.

overview.heading: Memory, artifacts, and a vertical museum journey.
overview.body: Midnight at the Pagoda began as a VR historical tour for the 2024 Digital Heritage Hackathon at the Great Bao'en Temple Museum, then developed into a Goldsmiths research thesis. The experience asks visitors to climb the Great Bao'en Temple Glazed Pagoda floor by floor, interact with artifacts, and learn temple history through movement, inspection, and embodied recall.

points.label: Prototype origin
points.body: Started as a VR heritage hackathon prototype for the Great Bao'en Temple Museum.

points.label: Research turn
points.body: Became an experimental environment for studying artifact interaction and memory retention.

points.label: Research output
points.body: Delivered as a VR app and research paper, with award and course outcomes recorded.

detailMedia.alt: Midnight at the Pagoda rendered scene

visualBreakMedia.alt: Midnight at the Pagoda exhibition proposal visual
visualBreakMedia.caption: The proposal reframed the pagoda as a journey through thresholds, artifacts, memory, and ascent.

sections.title: Why reconstruction was not enough
body: The surviving site can show foundations, fragments, and individual artifacts, but much of the pagoda's religious, social, and historical context has disappeared. A precise 3D replica would preserve appearance without necessarily helping visitors understand why the place mattered.
The design question became more specific: how could movement, touch, scale, and sound reconnect artifacts with their original use, while giving visitors an active role in building the story?

points.label: Context loss
points.body: Physical remains no longer carry the complete environment, rituals, and human relationships that once gave them meaning.

points.label: Passive interpretation
points.body: Static labels and visual reconstruction still leave the visitor outside the historical process.

sections.title: The climb became the interface
body: I organised the experience as an irreversible ascent. Each threshold changes the visitor's position, the available interaction, and the emotional register of the space. The route carries the narrative, so instruction can remain inside the environment rather than becoming a separate interface layer.

steps.label: Threshold
steps.title: Enter through the glazed arch
steps.body: Touch establishes the interaction language and moves the visitor from the museum into the reconstructed world.

steps.label: Foundation
steps.title: Follow artifacts into memory
steps.body: Scrolls, reliquaries, and light trails connect the underground chamber with historical scenes and distant places.

steps.label: Tower
steps.title: Act inside the historical account
steps.body: The visitor observes the city, handles a brush, and completes a mural rather than receiving the story as a caption.

steps.label: Summit
steps.title: Move from object to atmosphere
steps.body: Sound, incense, scale, and abstraction shift the experience from material history toward reflection.

media.alt: Annotated route through the pagoda foundation scene, from the entrance to the scroll collection
media.caption: Foundation route, first pass: the visitor crosses the room before the central artifact is revealed.

media.alt: Annotated route from the scroll collection to the central Ashoka pagoda model
media.caption: The return path changes after the artifact becomes active.

media.alt: Annotated route across stepping stones toward the Buddha at the summit scene
media.caption: At the summit, the route becomes slower, exposed, and ceremonial.

sections.title: Turning artifacts into interactions
body: Each interaction had to do two jobs at once: produce a clear runtime response and change how the visitor understood the artifact. The system therefore links physical action, spatial feedback, and narrative consequence.

mapping.response: A light path enters the historical image and opens a memory of Kew Gardens.
mapping.meaning: The museum object becomes a route into the pagoda's international history.

mapping.response: The object expands around the visitor and lifts them toward the next floor.
mapping.meaning: A change in scale turns close inspection into embodied transition.

mapping.response: Sound becomes visible and travels through the environment as light and movement.
mapping.meaning: An intangible ritual is represented through a response the visitor can see and influence.

media.alt: Storyboard showing the end-to-end visitor journey from transition space into narrative and interaction floors
media.caption: The end-to-end journey connects the physical waiting area, headset setup, narrative floors, and interaction floors.

sections.title: From hackathon prototype to research system
body: The project did not move directly from concept to thesis. A small team first built and presented a working prototype at the Digital Heritage Hackathon. Feedback from the live demonstration, expert review, and later academic critique exposed gaps in the narrative and informed a broader exhibition plan.

timeline.title: Prototype and field presentation
timeline.body: Built a minimum viable VR experience, presented it in a real event setting, and collected early qualitative feedback.

timeline.title: Research framing
timeline.body: Revisited the prototype through visual grammar, interaction meaning, and comparative case analysis.

timeline.title: Integrated exhibition plan
timeline.body: Expanded the tested interaction logic into a nine-floor narrative and a complete research thesis.

media.alt: The Midnight at the Pagoda team building and testing the VR prototype during the Digital Heritage Hackathon
media.caption: Prototype development during the 2024 Digital Heritage Hackathon.

media.alt: Ye Mai presenting the VR heritage project on stage at the Digital Heritage Hackathon
media.caption: Presenting the interaction concept and prototype.

media.alt: The project team discussing the VR prototype with an event reviewer
media.caption: The live setting produced early review and qualitative feedback.

sections.title: What the evidence supports
body: The project supports a clear claim about process: heritage interpretation can be designed through movement, interaction, and spatial composition rather than added as explanatory text after the environment is built. Its current evidence is strongest at the level of prototype quality, expert review, and research synthesis.

columns.title: Evidence on record
items: Best Use of Tech, Digital Heritage 2024
A working VR prototype and public presentation
77/100 in the Goldsmiths Research Project course
A completed research thesis and integrated exhibition plan

columns.title: Still to validate
items: Large-scale visitor response and long-term memory effects
Behaviour tracking across the complete nine-floor journey
Performance trade-offs on mobile headsets at exhibition scale

sections.closing: My role moved across narrative design, scene design, VR development, field presentation, and research synthesis.

projects.title: GAVIS VR
projects.tagline: A self-guided VR app for classroom English learning.
projects.detailHeading: A self-guided VR onboarding scene that teaches students gestures, safety, and hand-tracking before login.

overview.heading: End-to-end use before login
overview.body: GAVIS, an English learning app for shared classroom headsets, needed a first-use path before login. I built an onboarding scene around three rehearsed actions: pinch, controller-down, and safety.

points.label: Pinch practice
points.body: Uses the same UI button students meet in the interaction scene.

points.label: Controller-down guidance
points.body: Tells students when to put controllers away and continue with hand tracking.

detailBody: GAVIS, an English learning app for shared classroom headsets, needed a first-use path before login. I built an onboarding scene around three rehearsed actions: pinch, controller-down, and safety.
My work covered scene setup, prefab setup, flow logic, condition validation, gesture animation production, feedback triggers, flow navigation, headset QA, and performance validation.

detailSections.title: From Human Guidance to Self-Guided Onboarding
body: Before the onboarding scene was implemented, students went straight to login in a shared classroom headset. Without staff beside them, many did not know what GAVIS expected, when to put down controllers, how to pinch, or which safety notice applied to the classroom setup.

A passive instruction video could explain the idea, but an interactive onboarding panel fit VR better: learners could rehearse the same gestures and UI actions they would use in the app, making the first-use path more direct and intuitive.

detailSections.title: Teach By Doing
body: The core strategy was Condition-Gated Progression: students advance only after completing the intended physical or UI action.
That turns onboarding into a capability arc: understand GAVIS, put down controllers, use hands, practice pinch with the UI button, read the safety notice, then enter the app.

detailSections.title: A Validated Practice Loop
body: Each task panel combines an instruction, a validator, hint audio, success feedback, and progression. The scene waits when the learner struggles and confirms the moment when they succeed.
For the pinch target step, success is visible, audible, and spatial: target guidance, hand animation, success audio, VFX at the pinch position, UI state, and panel progression.

detailSections.title: XR Animation Built Inside Unity
body: The hardest craft problem was gesture guidance, which needed an in-Unity recording workflow instead of a traditional Blender animation pipeline.
Hand and controller motion was recorded in Play Mode, trajectories were mapped, sampling and interpolation were tuned, and reusable clips were baked for pinch and controller-down guidance.

mediaSlots.alt: Onboarding gesture animation production pipeline diagram
Controller-down guidance animation running in the onboarding scene
Pinch guidance animation running in the onboarding scene

detailSections.title: Students Used GAVIS on Their Own
body: After the onboarding scene was added, we ran a small pilot test with secondary school students using GAVIS in a classroom headset setup.

The first-use flow reached the goal it was built for: most students could learn the basic VR interaction language, move through onboarding, and enter GAVIS with little one-to-one staff guidance. Feedback from the pilot was positive.

observation.label: Pilot observation
observation.body: Onboarding shifted first use from human-led explanation to a self-guided rehearsal of the gestures students needed inside GAVIS.

projects.detailHeading: 一个研究文物交互如何影响观众记忆的 VR 文化遗产应用与研究论文。

overview.heading: 记忆、文物与垂直博物馆旅程。
overview.body: 佛塔的午夜最初是为 2024 Digital Heritage Hackathon 和大报恩寺遗址博物馆制作的 VR 历史导览原型，之后发展为 Goldsmiths 的研究论文。体验让观众逐层攀登大报恩寺琉璃塔，与楼层中的文物互动，并通过移动、观察和具身交互理解寺塔的建造历史、文化意义和材料遗产。
